name: Lalibela
scope: A mountain town in the Ethiopian highlands, home to eleven medieval churches carved DOWN into solid rock. T1: the churches are not built UP from blocks but hewn DOWN into the ground -- Bete Giyorgis (the Church of St George) is a perfect cross shape sunk about 12 metres into the earth, its roof at ground level and cut entirely from one single block of red volcanic rock. T2: King Lalibela ordered them in the late 12th-13th century to build a 'New Jerusalem' after Muslim conquests cut Ethiopian Christians off from pilgrimage to the Holy Land -- he even renamed a local stream the 'Jordan' (invert: the New-Jerusalem purpose is the answer). T3: the monolithic method -- masons dug trenches in a rectangle to free a block of rock, then carved it top-down, outside and inside, adding nothing; Biete Medhane Alem, with five aisles, is the largest monolithic (single-rock) church in the world. T4: the eleven churches are linked by a maze of trenches, tunnels, and passages opening onto hermit caves and catacombs, and remain a LIVING Ethiopian Orthodox pilgrimage site ~800 years on. T5: an old tradition holds that angels worked through the night to double the masons' daily progress -- label as LEGEND, the real wonder is the top-down carving into volcanic scoria over basalt.
source: UNESCO WHC list/18 (Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela); Wikipedia 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela' & 'Church of Saint George, Lalibela'; Britannica 'Lalibela'. (Grokipedia page fetch returned HTTP 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: scene-led -- open on the cross-shaped church sunk INTO the ground, never 'What is a monolithic church?'. The one picture a 10-year-old holds is a whole church carved downward from a single rock (T1 dinner-test payoff). Accuracy rail: it is cut from red volcanic SCORIA over basalt, not granite; keep 'monolithic' TAUGHT (carved from one piece) before it is tested. Every answer is a place-fact about THIS site. Distractors: other rock-cut sites (Petra, the Ajanta caves, Ellora) keep all four live. Mark the angels-at-night rung explicitly as LEGEND, not fact.

name: Aksum
scope: The ruined capital of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum in northern Ethiopia, famous for its field of giant carved stone pillars (stelae). T1: the stelae are single towering stones carved to look like multi-storey tower-houses, complete with false doors and rows of false windows -- the tallest standing one shows about thirteen 'floors'. T2: the Obelisk of Axum, 24 m tall and 160 tonnes of one solid stone, was looted by Italian troops on Mussolini's orders in 1937, stood in Rome for decades, and only returned to Aksum in 2005 (re-erected 2008) -- invert: the stolen-and-returned stone is the hook, the place is the answer. T3: DINNER TEST -- the Great Stele, 33 m and roughly 520 tonnes, is the largest single block of stone humans have ever TRIED to raise; it lies shattered where it fell, probably collapsing during the very attempt to stand it up. T4: the stelae marked the graves of Aksum's kings, and Aksum was a trading empire rich enough to mint its OWN gold coins -- one of the first states on Earth to do so, ~3rd century AD. T5: under King Ezana (~330s AD) Aksum became one of the first kingdoms anywhere to adopt Christianity, and Aksum's Church of St Mary of Zion claims to guard the Ark of the Covenant to this day (label as sacred CLAIM held on faith).
source: Wikipedia 'Obelisk of Axum' & 'King Ezana's Stele'; UNESCO WHC list/15 (Aksum); SFU Museum of Archaeology (Aksumite Stelae). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: the Great Stele's 'largest stone humans ever attempted' is the invert-the-wonder hook -> the answer is that it FELL and shattered during erection (T3 dinner-test). Accuracy rail: keep the three stelae straight -- standing Ezana's Stele 21 m, looted-and-returned Obelisk of Axum 24 m/160 t, shattered Great Stele 33 m/~520 t; do NOT conflate them. Stance: present Aksum as a FULL civilization (monumental engineering, its own coinage), never 'primitive'; RESPECT the Ark-of-the-Covenant claim on its own terms -- attribute it as a belief, no smug secular dismissal and no asserting it as proven. Distractors: other tall monuments/obelisks (Egyptian obelisks, Cleopatra's Needle) keep all four live.
history_overlap: Ezana's adoption of Christianity is a candidate history-bank episode; keep the geography answer a PLACE-fact about Aksum (the stelae, the coins, the St Mary of Zion site), not a biography of Ezana.

name: Great Zimbabwe
scope: A vast stone city in the hills of southern Africa, built by ancestors of the Shona people between the 11th and 15th centuries. T1: its enormous curving walls are stacked from millions of shaped granite blocks fitted together with NO mortar of any kind -- 'Zimbabwe' means 'houses of stone,' and the modern country took its name from these ruins. T2: the Great Enclosure -- a ring wall roughly 250 m around, up to 11 m high and 5 m thick -- is the largest ancient structure anywhere south of the Sahara (invert: the 'biggest south of the Sahara' superlative is the hook). T3: inside the Great Enclosure stands a solid Conical Tower about 9 m tall, shaped like a giant grain silo -- thought to symbolise a Shona king's granary and his power to feed and protect his people. T4: the city grew rich on GOLD and Indian Ocean trade -- Chinese porcelain, Persian glass, and coral have been dug from the site, proof it was plugged into a trade network reaching across the ocean. T5: HONEST HISTORY -- carved soapstone birds once crowned the walls; colonial-era Europeans (the explorer Karl Mauch and Cecil Rhodes' circle) refused to believe Africans built it and pushed a false 'Queen of Sheba / Phoenician' story to justify looting it, and today one of those Zimbabwe Birds flies on the national flag.
source: Wikipedia 'Great Zimbabwe'; Smarthistory 'Great Zimbabwe'; The Met (Great Zimbabwe essay); Britannica 'Great Enclosure'. (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: lead on the mortarless curving walls a kid can picture -> answer 'the country is named after them' (T1 dinner-test); do NOT open with 'What is the largest structure south of the Sahara?'. Stance (VISION-MANDATED): celebrate this as a FULL indigenous civilization built by the Shona; state the colonial denial plainly as the myth it was and land the payoff that the bird now flies on the flag -- honest history that reverses the insult. Accuracy rail: attribute the tower's granary meaning as the leading interpretation, not settled certainty. Distractors: other dry-stone / ancient African sites (Khami, Mapungubwe, Great Enclosure vs Hill Complex) keep all four live. Lane: the gold-trade rung links to Kilwa/Sofala as PLACES in a network -- don't duplicate Kilwa's ladder.

name: Timbuktu
scope: A fabled city of mud on the southern edge of the Sahara in Mali, once a hub where the desert met the river. T1: at Timbuktu, camel caravans traded blocks of SALT for GOLD almost weight for weight -- salt was so scarce in the tropics that it was cut in slabs from desert mines (Taghaza) and hauled hundreds of miles by camel. T2: the Djinguereber Mosque, built of mud and adobe in the 1320s (c. 1327) for the emperor Mansa Musa, still stands ~700 years later, its walls bristling with wooden beams; invert: the 'oldest mud mosque still standing here' wonder is the answer. T3: Timbuktu's Sankore and sister mosques formed one of the oldest centres of higher learning in Africa, drawing scholars to study law, astronomy, and medicine. T4: the city's real treasure was BOOKS -- hundreds of thousands of handwritten manuscripts kept in private family libraries, hard proof of a deep WRITTEN African scholarly tradition. T5: DINNER TEST -- in 2012-2013, when armed extremists seized Timbuktu and began burning manuscripts, the librarian Abdel Kader Haidara and helpers secretly smuggled around 350,000 manuscripts out of the city in trunks and boats down the river to Bamako to save them.
source: Wikipedia 'Djinguereber Mosque' & 'Timbuktu Manuscripts'; History.com 'How Timbuktu Flourished'; CNN (2022, Google digitization of Timbuktu manuscripts). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: open on the salt-for-gold desert trade a kid can picture; the manuscript rescue is the dinner-test payoff (T5). Accuracy rail: the mosque dates to the 1320s (~1327), rebuilt/maintained since -- say 'begun c.1327 and maintained' not 'unchanged since'; the ~350,000 figure and Haidara's rescue are well-documented. Lane border: SALT here is a geographic desert RESOURCE and trade good (weight-for-weight with gold), NOT a cooking ingredient -- keep the answer the place/trade fact, not seasoning. Stance: present Timbuktu as evidence of a sophisticated WRITTEN African civilization, correcting the 'Africa had no history' trope. Distractors: other Saharan/Sahel trade cities & mud mosques (Djenné, Gao, Agadez) keep all four live.
history_overlap: Mansa Musa's hajj and gold are a famous history-bank figure; keep the geography answer the PLACE (the mud mosque he built, the trans-Saharan salt-gold crossing, the manuscript libraries), not Musa's biography.

name: Djenné (Great Mosque)
scope: A trading town on the inland Niger delta in Mali, built almost entirely of mud. T1: the Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest MUD-BRICK building on Earth -- made of sun-dried mud bricks, sand, and palm-wood beams, not stone or concrete. T2: rows of wooden beams (toron) poke straight out of the walls everywhere -- they are both decoration AND permanent built-in scaffolding, footholds the masons climb to reach the upper walls. T3: DINNER TEST -- because rain slowly melts the mud, once a year the WHOLE TOWN replasters the mosque by hand in a single festive day, the crépissage, young men racing up the toron with baskets of wet mud (invert: the 'why does a giant building need replastering every year?' hook -> it is made of mud). T4: the current mosque was rebuilt in 1907 on the site of a 13th-century mosque founded by Djenné's king Koi Konboro; the mud plaster (banco) is mixed with rice husks and shea butter to help it grip and shed water. T5: next door, ancient Djenné-Djenno is one of the oldest known cities in sub-Saharan Africa, settled around 250 BC -- evidence of West African city life long before any outside contact.
source: Smarthistory 'Great Mosque of Djenné'; UNESCO WHC (Old Towns of Djenné); ReligionUnplugged & Bayt Al Fann (annual re-plastering / crépissage). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: the annual whole-town replastering is the dinner-test payoff (T3) -- lead with the puzzle 'why must an entire town re-mud a building every single year?' and let 'it is built of mud' be the reveal, never 'What is the largest mud building?'. Accuracy rail: the STANDING structure dates to 1907 (rebuilt on a much older site) -- don't imply the visible mosque is 700 years old; the toron are functional footholds, not just ornament. Distractors: other Sudano-Sahelian mud architecture (Djinguereber, Agadez minaret, Bobo-Dioulasso) keep all four live. Lane: banco's rice-husk/shea recipe is a building material, not a food -- keep the answer the place/architecture fact.

name: Cape Town & Table Mountain
scope: A city wedged between the Atlantic and a flat-topped mountain at the southern tip of Africa. T1: Table Mountain has a summit as flat as a tabletop, and a low cloud regularly pours over its edge and hangs there like a white 'tablecloth.' T2: that tablecloth forms when the moist south-east wind -- nicknamed the 'Cape Doctor' because it sweeps the city's air clean -- is forced up the slope and cools into cloud (invert: 'why does one mountain wear a permanent cloud?' -> the rising wind). T3: DINNER TEST -- the mountain is the heart of the Cape Floral Kingdom, the SMALLEST but richest of Earth's six great plant kingdoms; Table Mountain ALONE holds around 2,200 plant species -- more than the whole of Britain -- most of it a shrubland called fynbos. T4: the flat summit is ancient -- its sandstone was laid down roughly half a billion years ago, before animals had crawled onto land, and hundreds of millions of years of erosion planed the top dead flat. T5: HONEST HISTORY -- from the summit you look out to Robben Island in the bay, the prison island where Nelson Mandela was held about 18 of his 27 years before walking free in 1990.
source: Wikipedia 'Table Mountain'; Britannica 'Table Mountain'; Table Mountain Aerial Cableway info guide (geology & fynbos). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: open on the flat-topped mountain wearing a cloud (T1 picture); the Cape Floral Kingdom's richness (more species than all of Britain) is the dinner-test payoff (T3), with Robben Island the honest-history close (T5). Accuracy rail: teach 'fynbos' and 'floral kingdom' before testing; the sandstone is ~450-510 My old -- say 'roughly half a billion years,' don't overstate a single crisp number. Lane border: the Cape Floral Kingdom is the PLACE's biome/earth-fact (geography); do NOT drift into one plant's or animal's biology (that's the animal/plant lane) -- keep the answer the place-superlative. Stance (VISION-MANDATED on T5): present Robben Island / Mandela plainly and with dignity. Distractors: other flat-topped or floristic-rich places (Roraima tepui, mesas, the Cerrado) keep all four live.
history_overlap: Mandela's imprisonment on Robben Island is a candidate history-bank episode; keep the geography answer the PLACE (the island visible from the summit, the prison), not a full biography of Mandela.

name: Stone Town, Zanzibar
scope: The old Swahili-coast trading town on Zanzibar island, a maze of coral-stone alleys off the Tanzanian coast. T1: Stone Town is famous for hundreds of hand-carved wooden DOORS -- heavy, studded with brass spikes, each carved with symbols of the owner's trade, faith, and status. T2: DINNER TEST -- the brass spikes were copied from India, where such studs were meant to stop war ELEPHANTS from battering doors down; Zanzibar has no war elephants, so on the island they became pure decoration and a badge of wealth. T3: Zanzibar's Omani sultans made the island the world's leading CLOVE grower -- the 'Spice Island' -- and even shifted their capital here all the way from Arabia (invert: 'why would a sultan move his capital from Arabia to a small African island?' -> the spice/trade wealth). T4: HONEST HISTORY -- Stone Town held East Africa's largest slave market; today an Anglican cathedral stands on that exact site, its altar set where the whipping post once was, above preserved underground holding cells. T5: the House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib) was the first building in all of East Africa to get electric light and an elevator.
source: Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; Siyabona (Stone Town architecture / Zanzibari doors); UNESCO WHC (Stone Town of Zanzibar). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: the war-elephant door studs are the dinner-test payoff (T2) -- lead with 'why are these African doors covered in spikes?' and let the India/war-elephant origin be the reveal. Lane border: CLOVES here are a place CROP and the reason the island became a trade capital (geography), NOT a cooking ingredient -- keep the answer the place-fact ('Spice Island' / capital moved here), don't drift into recipes. Stance (VISION-MANDATED on T4): present the slave-market history honestly and plainly, cathedral-over-market as the sober reversal. Accuracy rail: the door-stud/war-elephant origin is a well-attested tradition -- fine to state as the doors' Indian-influence origin. Distractors: other Indian Ocean / Swahili trade towns (Lamu, Mombasa, Kilwa) keep all four live.
history_overlap: The East African slave trade is a candidate history-bank topic; keep the geography answer the PLACE (the market site, the cathedral built over it), not the trade's full economic history.

name: Gondar
scope: A former imperial capital in the Ethiopian highlands, nicknamed the 'Camelot of Africa.' T1: Gondar is startling because it is full of real stone CASTLES -- towers, battlements, and turrets -- looking like a slice of medieval Europe dropped into the Ethiopian mountains. T2: Emperor Fasilides built the first castle around 1636 and made Gondar Ethiopia's permanent capital, ending centuries of moving royal camps; the whole royal compound, Fasil Ghebbi, sits behind a 900-metre wall (invert: 'why did Ethiopia's emperors build a European-looking fortress-city?' -> Fasilides settling a fixed capital). T3: DINNER TEST -- the ceiling of Debre Berhan Selassie church is covered edge to edge with the winged faces of about 80 cherub angels, all gazing down at once -- one of the most famous painted interiors in Africa. T4: nearby, Fasilides' Bath -- a stone pool -- is filled just once a year for the Timkat (Epiphany) festival, when thousands of pilgrims plunge into the blessed water to renew their baptism.
source: UNESCO WHC list/19 (Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar Region); ICCROM (Debre Berhan Selassie angel ceiling); Brilliant Ethiopia (Gondar). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: lead on the surprise of stone castles in the Ethiopian highlands (T1); the 80-angel-face ceiling is the dinner-test payoff (T3). Accuracy rail: attribute the castle-founding to Fasilides ~1636; give the ceiling's angel faces as ~80 (the commonly cited count) without over-precision, and note the church itself is 17th-18th century. Stance: RESPECT the Timkat plunge as a living sacred rite, described on its own terms. Distractors: other fortified royal/monastic sites (Lalibela, Fasil vs Kuskuam, Ethiopian vs European castles) keep all four live.

name: Harar
scope: An ancient walled Muslim town on a plateau in eastern Ethiopia, a tangle of alleys inside a stone ring. T1: Harar Jugol is a whole town wrapped in a 5-metre stone wall pierced by just five gates, and inside it packs 368 narrow twisting lanes into barely one square kilometre. T2: Harar is counted by many Muslims as Islam's FOURTH-holiest city (after Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem) -- inside its walls stand 82 mosques, three of them from the 10th century, and over 100 saints' shrines (invert: 'why is this tiny Ethiopian town so sacred?' -> the fourth-holy-city status). T3: DINNER TEST -- every night a 'hyena man' sits just outside the wall and hand-feeds strips of meat, sometimes mouth to mouth, to wild spotted hyenas that trot in through drainage holes in the wall -- a tradition running back generations. T4: Harar's tall old houses have brightly painted, basket-hung interiors (Harari architecture), and the town has long been a famous highland trading and coffee-growing centre on the caravan route to the coast.
source: UNESCO WHC list/1189 (Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town); Museum of Wander (Harar); Dawan Africa (Harar as Islam's fourth holy city). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: the nightly hyena feeding is the dinner-test payoff (T3) -- lead with the scene of a man hand-feeding wild hyenas at the town wall. Lane border: the hyenas are an ANIMAL aside -- keep the answer the PLACE-tradition (the walled town where men feed wild hyenas by hand), NOT the hyena's biology or behavior (that belongs to the animal bank). Accuracy rail: '82 mosques / 102 shrines / 368 lanes / five gates' are UNESCO's figures; the fourth-holiest-city status is a widely held claim -- attribute it, don't assert it as universal. Distractors: other walled old towns / holy cities (Fez medina, Kairouan, old Sana'a) keep all four live.

name: Gorée Island
scope: A small rocky island off Dakar, Senegal, a memorial of the Atlantic slave trade -- HONEST HISTORY. T1: Gorée's pink-and-ochre House of Slaves (Maison des Esclaves) has a narrow 'Door of No Return' opening straight onto the open Atlantic -- the world's best-known memorial to the transatlantic slave trade. T2: DINNER TEST / the honest debate -- Gorée is a powerful SYMBOL, but historians disagree how many enslaved people actually shipped from this specific island: some Senegalese scholars say vast numbers passed through, while historian Philip Curtin argued the figure was far smaller (a few hundred a year at most), with most captives in the region leaving from busier river-mouth ports on the mainland (label DISPUTED, present BOTH honestly). T3: the island itself was fought over and traded between the Portuguese, Dutch, English, and French because its little harbour guarded the sea route around West Africa -- its real value was its POSITION on the Atlantic corner of the continent. T4: today Gorée is a UNESCO site and a place of pilgrimage and reconciliation -- presidents, popes, and Nelson Mandela have stood at its door -- and the memory it carries matters regardless of the exact count.
source: Wikipedia 'House of Slaves'; History News Network 'The Myth of Gorée Island'; Philip Curtin, 'The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census' (1969); UNESCO WHC (Island of Gorée). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: the honest historians' debate IS the ladder's dinner-test payoff (T2) -- present it truthfully from BOTH sides, neither erasing the memorial's meaning nor overstating the island's actual shipping volume. Stance (VISION-MANDATED): honest-both-ways on the slave trade; the anchor stays the PLACE (the island, the House, the Door, its strategic harbour). Accuracy rail: label the numbers DISPUTED explicitly -- attribute the millions-claim to Senegalese memorial tradition and the far-smaller estimate to Curtin; do not present either as settled. Distractors: other slave-trade sites / Atlantic forts (Elmina, Cape Coast Castle, Bunce Island) keep all four live.
history_overlap: The transatlantic slave trade is a major history-bank topic; the geography lane keeps the PLACE (the island, the memorial house, the harbour's strategic position), not the trade's overall history.

name: Lagos
scope: Africa's largest city, sprawled across islands and a lagoon on Nigeria's Atlantic coast. T1: Lagos is not built on solid ground but spread across ISLANDS, sandbars, and a huge coastal LAGOON -- its very name comes from the Portuguese word for 'lakes/lagoons.' T2: DINNER TEST -- in the Makoko district a whole neighbourhood of wooden houses stands on tall STILTS above the lagoon water, reached only by canoe, earning it the nickname 'the Venice of Africa' (invert: 'why do thousands of people live in houses standing IN the water?'). T3: long barrier islands and sand spits shield the city from the open Atlantic; the Yoruba original name for the place is Èkó, older than 'Lagos.' T4: Lagos was Nigeria's capital until 1991, when the government built a brand-new planned capital, Abuja, in the country's centre -- yet Lagos stayed the country's crowded economic heart, one of the fastest-growing megacities on Earth (roughly 15-20+ million people).
source: Wikipedia 'Lagos' & 'Makoko'; Britannica 'Lagos'; BlackPast (Abuja becomes capital, 1991). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: lead on the city built ON water -- islands and lagoon (T1); the Makoko stilt village is the dinner-test payoff (T2). Accuracy rail: the population is genuinely uncertain -- say 'roughly 15-20+ million' as a range, never a false-precise figure; the capital moved to Abuja in 1991. Keep answers place-anchored (the lagoon, the stilt village, the name Èkó, the capital move) -- avoid a bare 'largest city in Africa' superlative-pick as the answer. Distractors: other coastal/water-built or fast-growing cities (Venice, Ganvié stilt village, Abuja, Kinshasa) keep all four live.

name: Kilwa Kisiwani
scope: A small island off southern Tanzania that was once one of the richest cities of the medieval Swahili coast. T1: Kilwa's merchants grew fabulously wealthy by controlling the GOLD that flowed up the coast from the interior (via Sofala) -- a tiny island city that became a gateway for Indian Ocean gold. T2: the Great Mosque of Kilwa, built of coral stone with rows of domes and arches, was for centuries the LARGEST mosque in sub-Saharan Africa (invert: 'why is the biggest mosque south of the Sahara on a little island?' -> the gold-trade wealth). T3: DINNER TEST -- the Husuni Kubwa palace, a sprawling 14th-century cliff-top complex of over 100 rooms, had its own OCTAGONAL swimming pool cut into the rock above the sea. T4: the great traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1331 and called Kilwa one of the most beautiful cities he had ever seen; Kilwa minted its own coins, and its golden age ended when the Portuguese sacked the island in 1505.
source: Wikipedia 'Kilwa Kisiwani' & 'Great Mosque of Kilwa'; UNESCO WHC list/144 (Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara); World Monuments Fund (Historic Sites of Kilwa). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: the cliff-top palace with its own octagonal sea-view pool is the dinner-test payoff (T3). Stance (VISION-MANDATED): present Kilwa as a sophisticated FULL Swahili civilization -- coral architecture, its own coinage, an indoor pool -- never 'exotic' or 'primitive.' Accuracy rail: 'largest mosque in sub-Saharan Africa' is true UP TO the 16th century -- phrase it as 'for centuries,' not forever; Ibn Battuta's 1331 visit and the 1505 Portuguese sack are firm dates. Lane: the gold-from-the-interior rung links to Great Zimbabwe/Sofala as PLACES in a trade network -- don't duplicate the Great Zimbabwe ladder. Distractors: other Swahili coral towns (Stone Town, Songo Mnara, Gedi, Lamu) keep all four live.

name: Kano
scope: One of the oldest cities of West Africa, a Hausa trade capital in northern Nigeria. T1: Kano is ringed by ancient mud CITY WALLS, raised and extended over centuries (from around the 11th century) to guard a great trans-Saharan trade town at the desert's southern edge. T2: DINNER TEST -- the Kofar Mata dye pits, dug around 1498, are the OLDEST indigo-dyeing pits in Africa still in use: deep clay pits of near-black blue dye where cloth has been coloured by hand for over 500 years (invert: 'where has the same blue dye been made in the same pits for five centuries?'). T3: Kano's Kurmi Market, founded in the 15th century, was one of the great markets on the southern edge of the Sahara, trading indigo cloth, leather, and goods carried by camel caravan across the desert.
source: Wikipedia 'Kofar Mata Dye Pits' & 'Kano'; Kohan Textile Journal (522-year-old dye tradition); Google Arts & Culture (Kano tie-and-dye). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
framing_note: Voice: the 500-year-old indigo dye pits are the dinner-test payoff (T2) -- lead with 'where has the same blue dye been made in the same clay pits since ~1498?'. Lane: indigo dyeing is a CRAFT/industry genuinely born and sustained in THIS place (a made-here creation -> geography), and the answer stays a place-fact (the Kofar Mata pits, the walls, Kurmi market) -- do not stray into textile chemistry. Accuracy rail: the pits date to ~1498 ('over 500 years'); the walls are centuries-long constructions, not a single build date. Distractors: other ancient West African / Hausa trade cities & crafts (Timbuktu, Katsina, Benin City walls, Djenné) keep all four live.
